newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China April fuel imports to fall, but trend up.
newsitem.headline: China April fuel imports to fall, but trend up.

text.p: China's import demand for fuel oil is expected to drop in April, a sharply rising longer term trend should see imports surging again soon, Chinese oil industry sources said on Tuesday.
They said imports would fall in April to around 400,000 tonnes from an average 700,000 tonnes because of a double blow of rising short-term international prices and higher tariffs.

"It is just a psychological move as importers feel the pinch of higher import tariffs," said one trader. "Imports are expected to resume to normal levels starting May or June as Chinese oil demand is rising very rapidly."
Easier import terms led to a surge in imports during the winter months. March imports were 600,000 tonnes, trade sources said.
Analysts estimate that China's fuel oil demand is rising at five percent a year.

But imports are rising at a rate of more than 40 percent a year, fuelled partly by a move by state refiner Sinopec to gear its 38 refineries to produce more diesel at the expense of reduced output of gasoline and fuel oil.
According to customs figures, China produced 23 million tonnes of fuel oil in 1996, down about 15 percent from 27.2 million tonnes in 1995.
Imports in 1996 were 8.5 million tonnes, up significantly from six million tonnes in 1995, customs figures show.
But despite the rising imports, the trend could see a glitch in April as importers adjust to the new tariff.
On April 1, import tariffs on fuel oil double to 6.0 percent from 3.0 percent -- a temporary tariff set in November 1996 to encourage imports at a time when international prices hit a five-year high.
Since then, prices have fallen, but Chinese importers said they remained high enough to dampen demand.

High sulphur fuel oil prices in the benchmark Singapore market were $104 per tonne at the end of last week, up from $99 earlier in the week. However, they were sharply lower than $125 per tonne hit in November 1996.

Nevertheless, the April 1 rise in import tariffs will be a big cut in historical tariffs. For the first 11 months of 1996, fuel oil imports were taxed at 12 percent until the temporary 3.0 percent tariff was imposed.
Most fuel oil is used in China's power generation industry -- a sector growing at 10 percent per year.
